problem: Existing VLN agents encode only the current route history and observations, so each episode is handled in isolation. Pre-exploration and beam search improve generalization to unseen scenes but cost extra steps, back-propagation, or long trajectories.
motivation: A deployed robot typically executes a series of instructions in the same scene, so information from earlier episodes is free to reuse. The paper treats this cross-episode scene-level memory as a cheap way to balance generalization and efficiency, without changing the action space or adding inference cost.
key_idea: Keep a per-scene graph memory of visited viewpoints across episodes, where each node stores a pooled feature of its neighbouring views, and fuse it into each candidate view's representation (candidate enhancing) at every step.
insight: Scene-level memory that enriches each candidate node's features helps more than path-level memory or a separate graph-encoding branch. In Appendix A, graph encoding gave no unseen gain (SPL 60.9), while candidate enhancing with max pooling gave 63.2 against the HAMT baseline's 60.9. Memory re-initialized at every episode drops R2R val-unseen SPL from 64 to 51, so the agent really relies on the accumulated memory. ESceme* with a near-complete memory adds only about 1-2 SPL, so the agent has learned to use partial, progressively built memory.
method: Episodic scene memory graph: a per-scene graph G_Y that starts empty and gains a node for each newly visited viewpoint plus edges (weight 1) to existing nodes; it is preserved across episodes in the same scene and never sees the global graph.
Node feature: the pooled (max by default, or mean) offline ViT features of the node's navigable neighbour views, so it adds no extra computation.

Candidate enhancing (CE): for each of the K candidate views, retrieve its memory feature m_k (zero if not yet in memory) and fuse it with the plain feature via a 2-layer MLP on [m_k; f_k]; the result goes to the cross-modal encoder as the observation input.
Agent-agnostic backbone: built on HAMT (also on TDSTP), using text/history/cross-modal encoders of 9/2/4 layers and ViT-B/16 features; the action space is unchanged, with STOP as a zero vector.
Training: end-to-end mix of imitation loss (alpha=0.2) and A2C RL loss, 100K iterations, batch size 8, lr 1e-5 on a single V100.

Inference variants: single-run ESceme, where memory builds progressively as episodes are executed; ESceme*, where the memory is first filled by going through all episodes (upper bound, about 2x time).
Graph Encoding alternative (Appendix): a 3-WL GNN encodes the memory subgraph as a separate branch into the cross-modal encoder; less effective than CE.

setting.backbone: HAMT (also TDSTP) transformer architecture with ViT-B/16 features, trained end-to-end (IL+RL)
setting.model_size: about 651.5 MB of parameters for HAMT (+6.8 MB for ESceme)
setting.training_data: R2R / R4R / CVDN / RxR training splits with the HAMT pretrained initialization; no extra data
setting.observation: panoramic RGB (36 views, ViT-B/16 features) with orientation and navigable signals; scene ID and viewpoint IDs
setting.action_space: discrete nav-graph viewpoints (local candidates plus STOP)
setting.privileged: scene ID and viewpoint (location) IDs from the simulator are used to index and retrieve the memory; episodes are executed sequentially in the same scene (IVLN-like setting)

results: With HAMT as the backbone, ESceme reaches R2R val-unseen SR 68 / SPL 64 and test-unseen SPL 63, which beats HAMT (SPL 61 / 60) and TDSTP (63 / 61). GridMM has higher SR but longer trajectories. On R4R it improves SPL to 43.2 and CLS to 62.7 against HAMT's 40.6 and 57.7. On CVDN it reaches test GP 5.99 against HAMT's 5.58, first on the leaderboard, at about 1% extra parameters and 4.8% extra inference time.
limitations: Requires scene identity and exact viewpoint IDs from the simulator (a discrete-graph assumption), and a sequential multi-episode setting; the paper only sketches how to extend it to continuous or SLAM-based settings.

Fine-grained view distinctions remain hard (failure cases: dining vs living room, 'slight left'); the gain from a more complete memory is small, limited by architecture, the frozen vision encoder, and data scale.
Comparisons to single-episode baselines are not strictly like-for-like, since ESceme uses information from earlier episodes in the same test scene.
